after.example: A small control network uses managed static neighbor entries for critical peers.

before.expanded_definition: Best Current Practice 38 - helps prevent networks from sending traffic with fake source addresses.
before.learning_explanation: BCP 38 is a defensive measure described in the source as: Best Current Practice 38 - helps prevent networks from sending traffic with fake source addresses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Network boundary filtering intended to reduce traffic with forged source IP addresses.
after.mechanism: Reject outgoing or incoming packets whose claimed source is inconsistent with the legitimate connected network.
after.conditions: Useful at networks that originate spoofed reflection requests, with routing-aware deployment.
after.limitations: It does not stop every DDoS technique or filter forged packets originating outside the enforcing network.
after.example: A provider filters customer egress so a compromised host cannot claim arbitrary victim addresses.

before.expanded_definition: Sets rules that determine which network traffic is allowed or blocked.
before.learning_explanation: Firewall Rules is a defensive measure described in the source as: Sets rules that determine which network traffic is allowed or blocked. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Explicit policy deciding which network flows or packets may cross a boundary.
after.mechanism: Apply permitted addresses, services, connection states or application-aware conditions according to the firewall capability.
after.conditions: Useful for restricting unnecessary exposure and dropping identifiable unwanted traffic.
after.limitations: Overly broad rules, encrypted traffic and allowed compromised services limit effectiveness. Local filtering cannot repair a saturated upstream link.
after.example: An edge policy blocks an unnecessary exposed UDP service used in reflection abuse.

before.expanded_definition: Identity and Access Management - Manages who can access systems and what they are allowed to do.
before.learning_explanation: IAM is a defensive measure described in the source as: Identity and Access Management - Manages who can access systems and what they are allowed to do. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Systems and policies managing identities, credentials and their authorized access to resources.
after.mechanism: Issue, authenticate, authorize, review and revoke identities and permissions through defined lifecycle controls.
after.conditions: Useful for people, services and cloud functions when effective permissions are assessed rather than assumed.
after.limitations: An authenticated or validly assigned identity can still be overprivileged or compromised. Policy interactions can be complex.
after.example: A function receives a service identity allowed to read only its assigned storage location.

before.expanded_definition: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 - A modern Wi-Fi security standard that provides stronger wireless protection.
before.learning_explanation: WPA3 is a defensive measure described in the source as: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 - A modern Wi-Fi security standard that provides stronger wireless protection. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Modern Wi-Fi authentication and encryption using the appropriate WPA3 personal or enterprise configuration.
after.mechanism: SAE or enterprise authentication protects association under the selected deployment model, with required management protections.
after.conditions: Use compatible patched clients and access points and an assessed transition configuration.
after.limitations: WPA3 does not patch every implementation flaw, prevent jamming or certify endpoint integrity. Unsafe fallback can weaken a deployment.
after.example: An enterprise distributes verified authentication-server settings to managed wireless clients.

before.expanded_definition: Updates device software to fix security weaknesses and bugs.
before.learning_explanation: Firmware Patches is a defensive measure described in the source as: Updates device software to fix security weaknesses and bugs. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Vendor-supported changes that repair known defects in embedded device software.
after.mechanism: Verify update provenance, assess compatibility, deploy and confirm the required version and configuration.
after.conditions: Useful when an applicable fix exists for an access point, camera or other supported device.
after.limitations: Updates can disrupt service and do not guarantee removal of prior compromise. Unsupported devices may need replacement.
after.example: A tested access-point firmware update closes a documented implementation weakness.

before.expanded_definition: Makes sensitive operations take the same amount of time to reduce timing attacks.
before.learning_explanation: Constant Time is a defensive measure described in the source as: Makes sensitive operations take the same amount of time to reduce timing attacks. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Code designed to avoid leaking secrets through data-dependent execution behavior relevant to the platform.
after.mechanism: Use reviewed primitives without secret-dependent branches or memory access in sensitive paths.
after.conditions: Useful against certain timing and cache side channels in comparisons and cryptographic operations.
after.limitations: Scheduling noise does not establish constant-time behavior; compiler, hardware, power and fault channels require separate analysis.
after.example: A token verifier uses a suitable constant-time comparison rather than exiting on the first differing byte.

before.expanded_definition: Hardware Security Module - A secure device that protects and manages encryption keys.
before.learning_explanation: HSM is a defensive measure described in the source as: Hardware Security Module - A secure device that protects and manages encryption keys. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A dedicated cryptographic device or service boundary that protects keys and performs permitted operations.
after.mechanism: Keys can remain inside the module while access policy, auditing and protected cryptographic operations constrain use.
after.conditions: Useful when an assessed security boundary and key-custody requirement justify the module's assurance level.
after.limitations: A module may still be misconfigured or vulnerable; authorized misuse and side channels are not automatically eliminated.
after.example: A signing service requests a signature from an HSM without exporting the private key to application memory.

before.expanded_definition: Prevents multiple processes from changing the same resource at the same time.
before.learning_explanation: Mutex is a defensive measure described in the source as: Prevents multiple processes from changing the same resource at the same time. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A synchronization mechanism that lets only one participating execution path enter a protected critical section.
after.mechanism: Acquire the shared lock before reading and updating the related state, then release it safely.
after.conditions: Useful when all paths obey the same lock discipline and the protected invariant is correctly identified.
after.limitations: Locks can deadlock or fail across non-participating processes; locking one variable may not protect a multi-resource invariant.
after.example: Threads serialize updates to a shared account balance through one agreed lock.

before.expanded_definition: Makes an operation complete fully or not happen at all, preventing partial changes.
before.learning_explanation: Atomic Ops is a defensive measure described in the source as: Makes an operation complete fully or not happen at all, preventing partial changes. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Operations whose relevant effects are indivisible to competing participants under the stated consistency model.
after.mechanism: Use suitable atomic instructions or transactions to protect an entire security-relevant state transition.
after.conditions: Useful for preventing check-and-update races when the operation spans the required invariant.
after.limitations: Atomicity of individual reads does not make a compound workflow safe. Distributed transactions and isolation levels need separate design.
after.example: A database transaction verifies and deducts an available balance as one protected operation.

before.expanded_definition: Watches for signs that accounts or information may have appeared in a data breach.
before.learning_explanation: Breach Monitoring is a defensive measure described in the source as: Watches for signs that accounts or information may have appeared in a data breach. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Checking for evidence that organizational accounts or credentials have appeared in known exposures.
after.mechanism: Correlate reliable breach intelligence with accounts and trigger verification, reset or investigation as appropriate.
after.conditions: Useful for finding reuse exposure and initiating response after a third-party breach.
after.limitations: Coverage is incomplete and reports can be delayed or wrong. Monitoring does not revoke a credential by itself.
after.example: A confirmed exposure leads the identity team to invalidate affected secrets and check suspicious sign-ins.

before.expanded_definition: Uses a different password for each account to limit damage if one is exposed.
before.learning_explanation: Unique Passwords is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses a different password for each account to limit damage if one is exposed. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Using a distinct password for each account so one service's exposure does not unlock another.
after.mechanism: A password manager can generate and retain separate strong secrets rather than relying on human memorization of variations.
after.conditions: Useful for limiting cross-service credential stuffing after another service exposes reusable passwords.
after.limitations: It does not protect a credential stolen from the very service being attacked or a compromised password manager or endpoint.
after.example: A retail password leak cannot authenticate to the user's email account because its password is different.

before.expanded_definition: Watches for repeated failed login attempts that may indicate suspicious activity.
before.learning_explanation: Failed Login Monitoring is a defensive measure described in the source as: Watches for repeated failed login attempts that may indicate suspicious activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Collecting and analyzing failed authentication events across accounts, sources and time.
after.mechanism: Detect patterns such as many accounts receiving a few common guesses, not only repeated failures on one account.
after.conditions: Useful for spotting spraying and other online authentication abuse with adequate retention and response.
after.limitations: It is detection, not automatic prevention. Attackers may distribute activity or blend with ordinary user failures.
after.example: A security alert links low-rate failures across hundreds of accounts to a coordinated spraying campaign.

before.expanded_definition: Multi-Factor Authentication — requires more than one way to verify a user's identity.
before.learning_explanation: MFA is a defensive measure described in the source as: Multi-Factor Authentication — requires more than one way to verify a user's identity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Authentication using independent factors rather than repeated versions of the same secret type.
after.mechanism: Require an additional factor and protect enrollment, recovery and factor replacement; prefer phishing-resistant designs where appropriate.
after.conditions: Useful for reducing takeover using a stolen password alone.
after.limitations: Some methods can be phished or fatigued. MFA does not protect every existing session or cure a compromised endpoint.
after.example: A service requires a device-bound authenticator proof that a stolen password alone cannot provide.

before.expanded_definition: Turns off outdated features or systems that may have security weaknesses.
before.learning_explanation: Disable Legacy is a defensive measure described in the source as: Turns off outdated features or systems that may have security weaknesses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Removing deprecated negotiation options and legacy access paths that the system no longer needs.
after.mechanism: Configure services to reject unsupported versions, weak algorithms or unsafe fallback, then test required clients.
after.conditions: Useful when older options enable downgrade or insecure authentication paths.
after.limitations: Compatibility dependencies need assessment; disabling an option does not fix every vulnerability in the remaining implementation.
after.example: A service stops accepting an obsolete transport version after all required clients are tested.

before.expanded_definition: HTTP Strict Transport Security - Forces websites to use secure HTTPS connections instead of unsafe HTTP.
before.learning_explanation: HSTS is a defensive measure described in the source as: HTTP Strict Transport Security - Forces websites to use secure HTTPS connections instead of unsafe HTTP. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A browser policy directing future access to an origin through HTTPS and disallowing certain insecure fallbacks.
after.mechanism: The site sends a policy over a valid HTTPS connection; approved preload deployment can cover an initial visit.
after.conditions: Useful against some HTTP downgrade and cookie transport exposure in supporting browsers.
after.limitations: It does not authenticate a look-alike domain or repair every TLS version downgrade. Initial-visit and subdomain policy need planning.
after.example: A browser refuses to downgrade a known HSTS site to plain HTTP on a hostile network.

before.expanded_definition: Wireless Intrusion Prevention System - Detects and helps block unauthorized wireless devices or connections.
before.learning_explanation: WIPS is a defensive measure described in the source as: Wireless Intrusion Prevention System - Detects and helps block unauthorized wireless devices or connections. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Monitoring wireless infrastructure for unauthorized or suspicious activity and applying assessed response policies.
after.mechanism: Compare observed radios and configurations with approved inventory and investigate anomalies.
after.conditions: Useful for discovering rogue or impersonating access points with adequate sensor coverage.
after.limitations: False positives and blind spots exist; automatic disruption may cause outages or legal issues. Detection is not proof of malicious intent.
after.example: Wireless sensors locate an unapproved access point connected to an office network.

before.expanded_definition: Allows or blocks network devices based on their MAC addresses.
before.learning_explanation: MAC Filtering is a defensive measure described in the source as: Allows or blocks network devices based on their MAC addresses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Allowing or denying local network participation based on observed link-layer addresses.
after.mechanism: Compare a device's claimed MAC address with a configured list at a supported access point or switch.
after.conditions: Useful for limited administrative inventory controls when stronger authentication is also present.
after.limitations: MAC addresses are observable and spoofable. This does not authenticate an access point or reliably prevent a rogue AP.
after.example: A small isolated lab uses MAC lists as an inventory aid, not as its primary device identity control.

before.expanded_definition: Lets users enter information on a screen instead of using a physical keyboard.
before.learning_explanation: Virtual Keyboards is a defensive measure described in the source as: Lets users enter information on a screen instead of using a physical keyboard. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Input interfaces that let users select characters without typing them through a physical keyboard.
after.mechanism: They may bypass a simple hardware or software logger that captures only physical key events.
after.conditions: Useful only against a clearly defined input interception path and with appropriate accessibility design.
after.limitations: Screen capture, mouse recording and browser hooks can still capture input. They are not a general defense against a compromised endpoint.
after.example: A special-purpose kiosk avoids a simple hardware keystroke recorder but still requires tamper inspection.

before.expanded_definition: Detects and removes malicious software from a device.
before.learning_explanation: Anti Malware is a defensive measure described in the source as: Detects and removes malicious software from a device. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Tools that detect, block or remediate malicious software using signatures and other techniques.
after.mechanism: Inspect files, processes and behavior, then quarantine or trigger investigation under managed policy.
after.conditions: Useful where the tool has sufficient visibility and current detection capability.
after.limitations: Unknown, privileged or evasive malware can be missed. A clean scan does not prove that all compromise effects are removed.
after.example: An endpoint blocks a recognized credential-stealing program and alerts the response team.

before.expanded_definition: Limits how many requests can be made within a certain amount of time.
before.learning_explanation: Rate Limiting is a defensive measure described in the source as: Limits how many requests can be made within a certain amount of time. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Restricting request frequency or resource use over a defined interval.
after.mechanism: Enforce appropriate quotas before expensive work, using identities or other assessed grouping keys.
after.conditions: Useful for login guessing and application-resource exhaustion when enforcement occurs at the relevant boundary.
after.limitations: Distributed sources, shared addresses and expensive permitted requests complicate limits. Local limits cannot create upstream bandwidth.
after.example: An API rejects excessive per-token requests before allocating costly backend jobs.

before.expanded_definition: Distributes network traffic across multiple systems to keep services available.
before.learning_explanation: Load Balancers is a defensive measure described in the source as: Distributes network traffic across multiple systems to keep services available. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Spreading service traffic across multiple healthy instances or locations.
after.mechanism: Routing and health checks distribute work and support failover across available capacity.
after.conditions: Useful for legitimate demand, instance failures and some resource-exhaustion events.
after.limitations: An attacker can overwhelm shared dependencies or total capacity. A load balancer does not itself distinguish malicious requests.
after.example: A service shifts traffic away from a failing instance while maintaining capacity in another zone.

before.expanded_definition: Temporarily blocks an account after too many failed attempts.
before.learning_explanation: Lockouts is a defensive measure described in the source as: Temporarily blocks an account after too many failed attempts. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.display_name: Account lockouts and progressive login restrictions
after.definition: Controls limiting repeated authentication failures against an account.
after.mechanism: Temporarily restrict attempts or apply increasing delays with appropriate recovery and monitoring.
after.conditions: Useful against online password guessing where the service controls the authentication path.
after.limitations: Attackers can abuse lockouts for denial of service, and low-rate spraying may evade per-account thresholds. Offline guesses are unaffected.
after.example: A portal slows repeated failed attempts and provides a protected recovery route for legitimate users.

before.expanded_definition: A test that helps determine whether a user is a person rather than an automated program.
before.learning_explanation: CAPTCHA is a defensive measure described in the source as: A test that helps determine whether a user is a person rather than an automated program. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Tests intended to make automated interaction more costly or difficult.
after.mechanism: Present an assessed challenge when risk warrants it, using accessible alternatives and server-side verification.
after.conditions: Useful as supplementary friction in some automated-abuse workflows.
after.limitations: Challenges can be solved, relayed or bypassed and can exclude users. They are not a sole authentication or brute-force defense.
after.example: A signup service challenges suspicious automation while also enforcing quotas and abuse monitoring.

before.expanded_definition: Uses ordered numbers to detect missing, repeated, or replayed messages.
before.learning_explanation: Sequence Numbers is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses ordered numbers to detect missing, repeated, or replayed messages. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Ordered message identifiers used with verification state to reject duplicates or out-of-window messages.
after.mechanism: Authenticate the sequence field and maintain an appropriate acceptance window for the session.
after.conditions: Useful for replay protection in command and transport protocols.
after.limitations: Unauthenticated numbering can be altered; resets, wraparound and state loss can reopen replay paths.
after.example: A controller discards an authenticated command number it has already processed.

before.expanded_definition: One-Time Password - Uses a one-time code that becomes invalid after it is used.
before.learning_explanation: OTP is a defensive measure described in the source as: One-Time Password - Uses a one-time code that becomes invalid after it is used. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Values intended to be accepted only once for a defined authentication purpose.
after.mechanism: Bind a generated code to the intended operation and invalidate it after use with server-side state or protocol checks.
after.conditions: Useful for specific authentication or recovery flows with protected delivery and verification.
after.limitations: Codes can be stolen or relayed before use; time-limited is not automatically single-use. They do not protect arbitrary messages without binding.
after.example: A recovery code becomes invalid immediately after a verified password-recovery transaction.

before.expanded_definition: Records when an event or action happened to help detect suspicious activity.
before.learning_explanation: Timestamps is a defensive measure described in the source as: Records when an event or action happened to help detect suspicious activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Time values used with trusted clocks and protocol checks to constrain message age.
after.mechanism: Authenticate the timestamp and reject messages outside a defined window, usually with additional replay tracking.
after.conditions: Useful when devices can maintain appropriate time and tolerate a designed acceptance window.
after.limitations: A timestamp alone permits repeated messages within the window. Clock drift and rollback handling require design.
after.example: A device rejects a signed command that is too old and tracks accepted message identifiers within the allowed interval.

before.expanded_definition: Uses temporary values to identify or authorize a user or request.
before.learning_explanation: Tokens is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses temporary values to identify or authorize a user or request. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Unpredictable values used to distinguish legitimate state-changing browser requests from cross-site forgeries.
after.mechanism: Generate and validate tokens bound to the appropriate session or request context on the server.
after.conditions: Useful for applications that otherwise rely on automatically sent credentials such as cookies.
after.limitations: XSS, token leakage and missing validation undermine the design. A generic bearer token is not automatically an anti-CSRF token.
after.example: A profile-change form is rejected when its request lacks the expected session-bound anti-CSRF value.

before.expanded_definition: Limits when cookies can be sent with requests from other websites.
before.learning_explanation: Same-site Cookies is a defensive measure described in the source as: Limits when cookies can be sent with requests from other websites. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Browser rules controlling cookie transmission in cross-site request contexts.
after.mechanism: Choose an appropriate Strict, Lax or other supported policy and verify behavior for the application's flows.
after.conditions: Useful as one layer against some CSRF and cross-site cookie exposure.
after.limitations: It is not a complete CSRF defense, especially for same-site attacks or unsafe endpoint design. Compatibility and necessary cross-site workflows matter.
after.example: A site tests that a cross-site navigation cannot silently perform a sensitive state-changing operation.

before.expanded_definition: Protects RFID data by encrypting it so unauthorized users cannot easily read it.
before.learning_explanation: Encrypted RFID is a defensive measure described in the source as: Protects RFID data by encrypting it so unauthorized users cannot easily read it. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: RFID credentials using protected cryptographic operations rather than relying only on a readable static identifier.
after.mechanism: Challenge-response can prove possession of a tag secret while freshness checks reject simple recording and replay.
after.conditions: Useful when readers, credentials and key management support an assessed authentication design.
after.limitations: Encrypted stored data alone may still be clonable; relay attacks and compromised readers require additional consideration.
after.example: A replacement badge system rejects a copied serial number because the counterfeit cannot answer its fresh challenge.

before.expanded_definition: Blocks or reduces unwanted signals that could interfere with or expose communications.
before.learning_explanation: Shielding is a defensive measure described in the source as: Blocks or reduces unwanted signals that could interfere with or expose communications. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Materials or enclosures that reduce radio transmission through a physical boundary.
after.mechanism: Attenuate the relevant frequencies with appropriate coverage, installation and tested effectiveness.
after.conditions: Useful for limiting unintended RFID reads or reducing particular electromagnetic exposure.
after.limitations: Gaps, unsupported frequencies and handling outside the enclosure remain risks. Shielding does not make a cloned identifier unforgeable.
after.example: Sensitive contactless credentials are kept in a tested shielded holder when not in use.

before.expanded_definition: Uses passwords that are harder for attackers to guess.
before.learning_explanation: Complex Passwords is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses passwords that are harder for attackers to guess. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Choosing long, unique passwords and rejecting commonly used or compromised candidates.
after.mechanism: Use adequate length, blocklists and password managers rather than relying on predictable character substitutions.
after.conditions: Useful against likely-password guessing for secrets that must still be user-entered.
after.limitations: Forced composition recipes can encourage predictable patterns. Better selection does not prevent phishing or theft from an endpoint.
after.example: A user creates a unique generated password instead of a sports team name with a year suffix.

before.expanded_definition: Adds a unique random value to a password before it is securely stored.
before.learning_explanation: Salting is a defensive measure described in the source as: Adds a unique random value to a password before it is securely stored. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Adding a unique salt as input to the password-hashing process.
after.mechanism: Store the salt with the verifier so identical passwords do not share a reusable precomputed hash computation.
after.conditions: Useful with a suitable cost-tuned password KDF for stored verification records.
after.limitations: Salts are not secrets and do not block online guesses or make an individual weak password unguessable.
after.example: Two accounts using the same password have distinct stored verification values because their salts differ.

before.expanded_definition: Stores passwords using a hash combined with a unique random salt.
before.learning_explanation: Salted Hashes is a defensive measure described in the source as: Stores passwords using a hash combined with a unique random salt. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Stored password hashes computed using a different salt for each password record.
after.mechanism: Per-record salts defeat shared lookup tables and reveal less about identical user passwords.
after.conditions: Use with an appropriate slow or memory-hard KDF and protected migration procedures.
after.limitations: A salted fast hash can still be guessed rapidly. Salting is not encryption and does not stop online credential stuffing.
after.example: A legacy application migrates unsalted hashes to a versioned salted password-verifier format.

before.expanded_definition: Makes password hashing slower to make large numbers of guesses harder.
before.learning_explanation: Key Stretching is a defensive measure described in the source as: Makes password hashing slower to make large numbers of guesses harder. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Deliberately expensive derivation that increases the cost of testing each password guess.
after.mechanism: Apply a suitable KDF with measured CPU and, where appropriate, memory cost and unique salts.
after.conditions: Useful against offline guessing when parameters balance security and authentication capacity.
after.limitations: It does not add entropy to a weak password or prevent online attacks by itself. Excessive cost can create service-exhaustion risks.
after.example: A password service periodically reassesses its KDF cost as hardware and operational capacity change.

before.expanded_definition: Requires users to change their passwords or credentials when needed.
before.learning_explanation: Mandatory Changes is a defensive measure described in the source as: Requires users to change their passwords or credentials when needed. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Requiring changes when defaults, exposure or recovery make an existing secret unsafe.
after.mechanism: Provision unique initial credentials, disable shared defaults and replace known compromised credentials through verified workflows.
after.conditions: Useful before device deployment and after evidence of exposure.
after.limitations: Arbitrary periodic changes without evidence are not a universal best practice and can encourage weak patterns. Rotation alone does not repair an active compromise.
after.example: A device cannot enter production until its published factory administrator credential is removed.

before.expanded_definition: Removes unnecessary features and settings to make a system more secure.
before.learning_explanation: Hardening is a defensive measure described in the source as: Removes unnecessary features and settings to make a system more secure. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Reducing unnecessary services, unsafe defaults and excess administrative exposure.
after.mechanism: Apply a reviewed baseline, remove unused functions and verify effective configuration after deployment.
after.conditions: Useful for reducing default-password exposure and avoidable attack surface.
after.limitations: A hardened baseline can drift and does not patch every unknown vulnerability. Hardening must respect operational needs.
after.example: An appliance's remote administration is restricted and unused accounts and services are disabled.

before.expanded_definition: Secure Hash Algorithm 3 - A secure hashing method used to create a unique digital fingerprint of data.
before.learning_explanation: SHA-3 is a defensive measure described in the source as: Secure Hash Algorithm 3 - A secure hashing method used to create a unique digital fingerprint of data. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A standardized family of cryptographic hash and extendable-output functions.
after.mechanism: A selected variant produces a digest for a specified security purpose without a shared secret.
after.conditions: Useful for appropriate integrity or cryptographic constructions when the variant and output size meet the requirement.
after.limitations: An unkeyed digest does not authenticate its sender. SHA-3 alone is not a password-storage scheme or a fix for every collision-sensitive design.
after.example: A protocol uses a reviewed SHA-3 variant as one component of its specified construction.

before.expanded_definition: Produces a longer security value, making guessing or cracking more difficult.
before.learning_explanation: Longer Output is a defensive measure described in the source as: Produces a longer security value, making guessing or cracking more difficult. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Choosing an output size that supplies the required work factor for the particular primitive and threat.
after.mechanism: For ideal n-bit hashes, generic collision search is about 2^(n/2), distinct from an n-bit preimage target.
after.conditions: Useful when designing identifiers or hashes that actually require collision resistance.
after.limitations: Length does not rescue a broken algorithm, poor randomness or an unsuitable protocol. Password strength is a separate property.
after.example: A toy short digest is replaced with an appropriately sized modern hash for document integrity checks.

before.expanded_definition: Checks that information, people, or actions are genuine and correct.
before.learning_explanation: Verification is a defensive measure described in the source as: Checks that information, people, or actions are genuine and correct. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Checking a claimed fact or requested action against separately trusted evidence.
after.mechanism: Confirm identity, intent and relevant details through known channels or approved records.
after.conditions: Useful for financial changes, support requests and software release decisions when the procedure is specific.
after.limitations: A vague instruction to verify is not a technical control until the evidence and procedure are defined.
after.example: Accounts payable confirms a bank-detail change using the supplier's established phone number.

before.expanded_definition: Teaches people to recognize tricks used to manipulate them.
before.learning_explanation: Social Engineering Training is a defensive measure described in the source as: Teaches people to recognize tricks used to manipulate them. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Practice in recognizing manipulation and using safe challenge and escalation procedures.
after.mechanism: Teach staff to pause, verify and report requests despite urgency, rewards or apparent authority.
after.conditions: Useful for pretexting and quid-pro-quo approaches with practical support from management.
after.limitations: Training does not authenticate a requester or block malware. Staff need a process they can actually follow under pressure.
after.example: A help-desk exercise rehearses refusing password requests while offering a legitimate recovery route.

before.expanded_definition: Requires visitors to be accompanied in restricted areas.
before.learning_explanation: Escort Policies is a defensive measure described in the source as: Requires visitors to be accompanied in restricted areas. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Rules requiring an authorized sponsor to accompany and account for visitors in controlled areas.
after.mechanism: Define access scope, check-in, supervision and safe escalation when a visitor separates from the escort.
after.conditions: Useful for visitors whose limited authorization does not permit independent movement.
after.limitations: A written rule without staffing and compliance does not enforce access. Emergency safety and accessibility remain essential.
after.example: A contractor is escorted between the reception desk and an approved equipment room.

before.expanded_definition: Uses stronger locks designed to resist unauthorized entry.
before.learning_explanation: High-Security Locks is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses stronger locks designed to resist unauthorized entry. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Locks designed and assessed for specified resistance to manipulation and unauthorized opening.
after.mechanism: Use an appropriate cylinder, protected installation and controlled key management as part of the door assembly.
after.conditions: Useful where mechanical access resistance is required and the selected assurance level matches the risk.
after.limitations: No lock is invulnerable; weak frames, copied keys and alternate entrances may bypass the cylinder.
after.example: A restricted store installs a rated cylinder and tracks authorized key issuance.

before.expanded_definition: Uses electronic security systems to control or monitor access.
before.learning_explanation: Electronic Security is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses electronic security systems to control or monitor access. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Electronic systems controlling or recording physical entry and related security events.
after.mechanism: Readers, door controllers, sensors and audit records enforce a defined access policy and support response.
after.conditions: Useful with reliable power, safe egress, protected credentials and maintained equipment.
after.limitations: A door reader does not necessarily strengthen a mechanical lock or prevent tailgating. Controllers themselves require security.
after.example: An entry controller logs a door opening and checks the presented credential against current access rights.

before.expanded_definition: Checks that information comes from a trustworthy and reliable source.
before.learning_explanation: Verify Sources is a defensive measure described in the source as: Checks that information comes from a trustworthy and reliable source. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Checking a warning, instruction or incident claim against independently trusted evidence.
after.mechanism: Consult genuine vendor advisories, internal security staff and original evidence rather than forwarding rumors.
after.conditions: Useful for hoaxes and misleading security instructions before taking disruptive action.
after.limitations: A trusted source can be mistaken or outdated; verify applicability and context rather than treating reputation as proof.
after.example: Staff verify an alarming deletion instruction with the security team before touching system files.

before.expanded_definition: Incident Response Plans - Provides steps for responding to and recovering from security incidents.
before.learning_explanation: IR Plans is a defensive measure described in the source as: Incident Response Plans - Provides steps for responding to and recovering from security incidents. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Prepared responsibilities and procedures for identifying, containing, investigating and recovering from incidents.
after.mechanism: Define escalation routes, evidence handling, communications and tested recovery decisions.
after.conditions: Useful when personnel exercise the plan and have authority and resources to act.
after.limitations: A document alone neither detects nor blocks an incident. Rigid procedures can fail when the real situation differs.
after.example: An exercised response plan coordinates containment and communications during a suspected ransomware incident.

before.expanded_definition: Controls and checks traffic entering or leaving a network.
before.learning_explanation: Gateways is a defensive measure described in the source as: Controls and checks traffic entering or leaving a network. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Boundary services that mediate and inspect a defined class of traffic.
after.mechanism: An email or web gateway can enforce content rules, scan objects and route suspicious activity for review.
after.conditions: Useful when the gateway's specific capability matches a documented delivery path.
after.limitations: The broad label does not imply all-purpose protection. Encrypted visibility, direct paths and unknown threats limit coverage.
after.example: A mail gateway quarantines a known malicious attachment associated with a ransomware campaign.

before.expanded_definition: Updates software to fix security weaknesses and bugs.
before.learning_explanation: Patching is a defensive measure described in the source as: Updates software to fix security weaknesses and bugs. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: The process of applying and verifying fixes for known software defects.
after.mechanism: Prioritize exposure, test operational effects, deploy trusted fixes and confirm vulnerable versions are removed.
after.conditions: Useful when a relevant vendor or maintainer fix exists.
after.limitations: Patching does not retroactively undo theft or persistence and cannot fix a flaw for which no remedy exists.
after.example: An exposed service receives a verified security patch after its risk and dependencies are assessed.

before.expanded_definition: Checks systems and practices to find security weaknesses.
before.learning_explanation: Assessments is a defensive measure described in the source as: Checks systems and practices to find security weaknesses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Structured evaluation of a supplier, service or system's relevant risks and practices.
after.mechanism: Review evidence, dependencies, development practices and response capability, then track specific findings.
after.conditions: Useful for selecting and monitoring supply-chain relationships according to their actual exposure.
after.limitations: A favorable assessment is not a guarantee of future security and may miss hidden compromise. Findings need enforceable follow-up.
after.example: A software buyer examines build provenance and incident notification commitments before adopting a dependency.

before.expanded_definition: Uses a digital signature to prove who created or approved data.
before.learning_explanation: Signing is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses a digital signature to prove who created or approved data. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Cryptographic checks tying signed content to a key identity and detecting later modification.
after.mechanism: Verify the signature with an independently trusted key and check release context and publisher identity.
after.conditions: Useful for software packages and update authenticity when the signing process is protected.
after.limitations: A valid signature does not prove benign behavior; compromised publishers or signing keys can sign malicious code.
after.example: An updater rejects a package altered by a mirror because its signature no longer matches the trusted release.

before.expanded_definition: Uses patterns and clues to identify possible threats.
before.learning_explanation: Heuristics is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses patterns and clues to identify possible threats. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Rules or models that infer suspicious behavior from patterns rather than only exact known signatures.
after.mechanism: Evaluate activity such as abnormal process chains or exploit-like behavior and escalate assessed matches.
after.conditions: Useful for finding some new variants or unknown exploits when relevant observations are available.
after.limitations: False positives, evasion and blind spots remain. It does not guarantee detection of a zero-day exploit.
after.example: An endpoint flags unusual child-process behavior even though the payload has no known hash signature.

before.expanded_definition: Uses information about known threats to help detect and prevent attacks.
before.learning_explanation: Threat Intel is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses information about known threats to help detect and prevent attacks. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Assessed information about adversaries, techniques, vulnerabilities or indicators that informs security decisions.
after.mechanism: Collect context, evaluate reliability and relevance, then connect intelligence to monitoring and response.
after.conditions: Useful for prioritization, hunting and detection updates when information is timely and applicable.
after.limitations: An indicator can be stale, shared or misleading; intelligence is not automatic blocking and cannot describe every unknown exploit.
after.example: A confirmed campaign report helps a team investigate a specific suspicious endpoint pattern.

before.expanded_definition: Completely separates a system from other networks to prevent network-based attacks.
before.learning_explanation: Air-Gapping is a defensive measure described in the source as: Completely separates a system from other networks to prevent network-based attacks. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: An architecture separating a system from direct network connections to other environments.
after.mechanism: Remove intended electronic network paths and control media transfer, maintenance and human access routes.
after.conditions: Useful where operational and safety needs permit a carefully maintained isolation boundary.
after.limitations: Removable media, laptops, supply-chain compromise and unofficial bridges can cross the gap. Claimed isolation must be verified.
after.example: A sensitive control system exchanges approved files only through a controlled transfer procedure.

before.expanded_definition: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition Firewalls - Protects industrial control systems by filtering their network traffic.
before.learning_explanation: SCADA Firewalls is a defensive measure described in the source as: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition Firewalls - Protects industrial control systems by filtering their network traffic. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Network boundary enforcement designed for assessed industrial control environments.
after.mechanism: Restrict allowed communication and, where supported, inspect relevant industrial protocol operations.
after.conditions: Useful between engineering, supervisory and process zones when rules are developed with operations and safety staff.
after.limitations: An unsafe rule can disrupt physical processes. Firewalls do not replace controller hardening, recovery or independent safety systems.
after.example: A plant boundary allows only approved engineering paths and rejects unnecessary controller access.

before.expanded_definition: Separates a network into sections to help stop threats from spreading.
before.learning_explanation: Segmentation is a defensive measure described in the source as: Separates a network into sections to help stop threats from spreading. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Dividing a network into security zones with controlled communication between them.
after.mechanism: Define allowed paths and enforce them through suitable routing, firewall or equivalent policy.
after.conditions: Useful for limiting lateral movement and reducing blast radius across workloads or device fleets.
after.limitations: An unconstrained VLAN is not sufficient isolation. Permitted vulnerable services and shared management paths can bridge zones.
after.example: An IoT camera zone cannot initiate connections to employee workstations.

before.expanded_definition: Blocks unauthorized network traffic from reaching protected systems.
before.learning_explanation: Firewall is a defensive measure described in the source as: Blocks unauthorized network traffic from reaching protected systems. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Enforcement devices or host controls that permit or block traffic according to configured policy.
after.mechanism: Restrict unnecessary services and crossings between network security boundaries.
after.conditions: Useful for reducing reachable paths and limiting propagation through unwanted services.
after.limitations: Allowed flows may carry attacks; policy errors and encrypted visibility limits remain. A firewall does not patch a vulnerable host.
after.example: A host firewall blocks an unused service that a worm otherwise could reach.

before.expanded_definition: Intrusion Prevention System - Detects and automatically blocks suspicious network activity.
before.learning_explanation: IPS is a defensive measure described in the source as: Intrusion Prevention System - Detects and automatically blocks suspicious network activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Controls that inspect activity and can block traffic matching supported attack conditions.
after.mechanism: Apply signatures or behavioral rules inline at an assessed enforcement point.
after.conditions: Useful against known exploit patterns with appropriate tuning and sufficient visibility.
after.limitations: False positives can interrupt service, and evasion or encrypted traffic can hide attacks. It does not replace patching.
after.example: An IPS rejects a recognized exploit request targeting an unpatched service while remediation is arranged.

before.expanded_definition: Security-Enhanced Linux - Uses strict security rules to control what applications and users can access.
before.learning_explanation: SELinux is a defensive measure described in the source as: Security-Enhanced Linux - Uses strict security rules to control what applications and users can access. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A Linux mandatory access-control system enforcing policy beyond ordinary discretionary permissions.
after.mechanism: Labels and policy rules constrain which resources and operations a process may use.
after.conditions: Useful for limiting container and host process access when enforcing mode and appropriate policy are maintained.
after.limitations: Permissive mode, overly broad policy and kernel vulnerabilities can undermine confinement. It does not make privileged containers universally safe.
after.example: A container process is denied access to host files outside its approved SELinux policy.

before.expanded_definition: Separates processes and resources so applications cannot easily interfere with each other.
before.learning_explanation: Namespaces is a defensive measure described in the source as: Separates processes and resources so applications cannot easily interfere with each other. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Operating-system mechanisms providing separated views of processes, mounts, networks or other resources.
after.mechanism: Assign workloads to appropriately configured namespaces to reduce unintentional sharing and visibility.
after.conditions: Useful as one component of container isolation on a supported patched host.
after.limitations: Namespaces do not alone provide a complete security boundary; capabilities, mounts, host sockets and kernel vulnerabilities matter.
after.example: A container has its own process and mount views while separate policy restricts privileged operations.

before.expanded_definition: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance — helps verify that emails really come from the claimed domain.
before.learning_explanation: DMARC is a defensive measure described in the source as: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance — helps verify that emails really come from the claimed domain. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.display_name: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
after.definition: Email-domain policy and reporting based on aligned SPF or DKIM results.
after.mechanism: A domain publishes policy and receivers assess alignment with the visible From domain under DMARC rules.
after.conditions: Useful against some unauthorized use of a protected domain in email, with carefully deployed enforcement.
after.limitations: It does not certify message content, stop look-alike domains or prevent abuse of a compromised legitimate account.
after.example: A company progresses to an enforced DMARC policy after reviewing legitimate mail flows and reports.

before.expanded_definition: Rules and checks that help prevent unauthorized financial activity.
before.learning_explanation: Financial Controls is a defensive measure described in the source as: Rules and checks that help prevent unauthorized financial activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Procedures that constrain how payments and account-detail changes are approved.
after.mechanism: Use independent verification, separation of duties, transaction limits and reconciled records.
after.conditions: Useful when deceptive communications attempt to turn a valid business workflow into fraud.
after.limitations: Collusion, weak exception paths and compromised approvers can undermine the process. Approval does not replace account security.
after.example: A changed payee requires confirmation through a known supplier contact and a second authorized approver.

before.expanded_definition: Trains executives to recognize and avoid targeted cyber threats.
before.learning_explanation: Exec Training is a defensive measure described in the source as: Trains executives to recognize and avoid targeted cyber threats. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Training adapted to high-value roles, authority pressure and sensitive business decisions.
after.mechanism: Practice delegation, payment verification and secure handling of board or acquisition material with relevant staff.
after.conditions: Useful for executives and assistants targeted by tailored deception.
after.limitations: Role-specific training does not override the need for technical controls or independent transaction checks.
after.example: An executive assistant practices challenging an urgent request that claims normal approvals must be skipped.

before.expanded_definition: Steps used to confirm that information, people or actions are legitimate.
before.learning_explanation: Verification Protocols is a defensive measure described in the source as: Steps used to confirm that information, people or actions are legitimate. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Documented steps for confirming a sensitive request through evidence independent of its delivery channel.
after.mechanism: Use established contact information, dual approval or separately authenticated records before accepting changed instructions.
after.conditions: Useful for transfers, credential recovery and privileged access changes.
after.limitations: A second channel controlled by the same attacker is not independent. Procedures need exceptions that cannot silently bypass verification.
after.example: Finance confirms altered supplier bank details using the supplier's pre-existing verified contact record.

before.expanded_definition: Limits sensitive information to only authorized users.
before.learning_explanation: Restricted Data Access is a defensive measure described in the source as: Limits sensitive information to only authorized users. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Limiting access to valuable data according to verified business needs.
after.mechanism: Apply resource-specific permissions, review grants and log sensitive retrieval or export.
after.conditions: Useful for reducing the reach of a compromised or deceived executive or other user.
after.limitations: It does not establish whether a communication is genuine or stop misuse of legitimately accessible data.
after.example: A transaction team limits acquisition documents to approved participants instead of a broad executive group.

before.expanded_definition: Controls which network ports are allowed to accept connections.
before.learning_explanation: Firewall Ports is a defensive measure described in the source as: Controls which network ports are allowed to accept connections. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Restricting which services accept or initiate network connections through firewall policy.
after.mechanism: Close unused listening services and apply assessed ingress and egress rules.
after.conditions: Useful for reducing unnecessary access paths to remote-control services.
after.limitations: A Trojan may use an allowed outbound connection or trusted service; port blocking alone is not malware cleanup.
after.example: A workstation policy denies unneeded inbound remote-control ports and monitors unexpected outbound sessions.

before.expanded_definition: Detects activity that is unusual compared with normal behavior.
before.learning_explanation: Anomaly Detection is a defensive measure described in the source as: Detects activity that is unusual compared with normal behavior. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Identifying observations that differ from a defined expected pattern.
after.mechanism: Compare activity with an assessed baseline or model and send meaningful deviations for investigation.
after.conditions: Useful for unusual destinations, process chains or identity activity when context is available.
after.limitations: An unusual event is not necessarily malicious, and attackers can imitate normal behavior. Baselines require maintenance.
after.example: A workstation contacting a new external control endpoint at unusual hours triggers review.

before.expanded_definition: Separates a device, system or process to prevent a problem from spreading.
before.learning_explanation: Isolation is a defensive measure described in the source as: Separates a device, system or process to prevent a problem from spreading. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Separating a suspected compromised system from sensitive resources while preserving appropriate response access.
after.mechanism: Restrict network paths, invalidate sessions where needed and use trusted systems for recovery decisions.
after.conditions: Useful for containing malware and avoiding sensitive work in a compromised browser or endpoint.
after.limitations: Isolation is not eradication; it can disrupt business and must preserve safety and evidence needs.
after.example: A suspected infected laptop is isolated from production access while responders collect evidence.

before.expanded_definition: Redirects suspicious network traffic to a controlled system for investigation.
before.learning_explanation: Sink Holing is a defensive measure described in the source as: Redirects suspicious network traffic to a controlled system for investigation. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Redirecting selected malicious infrastructure traffic to a controlled defensive destination.
after.mechanism: Use appropriate legal and technical authority to alter resolution or routing for a known command endpoint.
after.conditions: Useful for disrupting some botnet control channels and identifying affected clients.
after.limitations: Alternative command paths and embedded addresses can bypass it. Sinkholing does not remove malware and must not capture unrelated traffic.
after.example: A coordinated defender operation redirects a botnet domain to a monitored defensive server.

before.expanded_definition: (New Technology Local Area Network) Turns off an older authentication system that has known security weaknesses.
before.learning_explanation: Disable NT LAN Manager is a defensive measure described in the source as: (New Technology Local Area Network) Turns off an older authentication system that has known security weaknesses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Reducing or eliminating an assessed Windows NTLM authentication path.
after.mechanism: Inventory dependencies, audit usage and enforce appropriate restrictions while migrating required services.
after.conditions: Useful against NTLM-specific credential reuse when supported alternatives and compatibility have been verified.
after.limitations: It can break legacy services and does not stop Kerberos ticket/key abuse or all credential theft. Some paths may remain unless explicitly covered.
after.example: An organization retires NTLM for a tested service and verifies that fallback is no longer accepted.

before.expanded_definition: Uses trusted tickets to securely verify users and services on a network.
before.learning_explanation: Kerberos is a defensive measure described in the source as: Uses trusted tickets to securely verify users and services on a network. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A ticket-based network authentication protocol using a trusted key distribution service.
after.mechanism: Clients obtain and present service tickets according to domain identity and trust policy.
after.conditions: Useful in appropriately managed environments as part of reducing legacy authentication exposure.
after.limitations: Kerberos is not a universal pass-the-hash remedy; stolen keys or tickets, weak delegation and NTLM fallback remain risks.
after.example: A service accepts properly validated Kerberos tickets after its authentication dependencies are reviewed.

before.expanded_definition: Role-Based Access Control — gives users access based on their assigned role.
before.learning_explanation: RBAC is a defensive measure described in the source as: Role-Based Access Control — gives users access based on their assigned role. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Authorization in which permissions are assigned to roles and identities receive approved role memberships.
after.mechanism: Enforce the role's permitted operations at resource boundaries and review membership lifecycle.
after.conditions: Useful for managing consistent job-based access in applications and cluster APIs.
after.limitations: Overbroad roles, inherited rights and compromised members can still cause harm. RBAC does not enforce every workload security setting.
after.example: A cluster user can inspect workloads but cannot create privileged administrative resources.

before.expanded_definition: Sets security rules for containers running inside a Kubernetes environment.
before.learning_explanation: Pod Policies is a defensive measure described in the source as: Sets security rules for containers running inside a Kubernetes environment. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Rules that assess workload security settings before resources are accepted into a cluster.
after.mechanism: Use supported controls such as Pod Security Admission and appropriate admission policy to restrict privileged workloads and unsafe host access.
after.conditions: Useful for new or changed workloads together with API authorization and runtime protection.
after.limitations: The removed PodSecurityPolicy API should not be deployed as a current feature. Admission policy does not fix every running workload or kernel flaw.
after.example: A cluster rejects a manifest requesting prohibited host privileges under its enforced workload standard.

before.expanded_definition: Keeps software and systems current to fix bugs and security weaknesses.
before.learning_explanation: Updates is a defensive measure described in the source as: Keeps software and systems current to fix bugs and security weaknesses. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Maintaining components through verified supported releases that correct known defects.
after.mechanism: Inventory versions, assess applicability, test where needed and verify deployment of the required update.
after.conditions: Useful when a known security flaw has a supported fix.
after.limitations: An update is not proof that a previously compromised device is clean; unsupported products may require replacement.
after.example: A camera fleet receives a tested vendor release addressing a remotely exploitable service flaw.

before.expanded_definition: Checks whether a message really comes from the claimed sender.
before.learning_explanation: Sender Verification is a defensive measure described in the source as: Checks whether a message really comes from the claimed sender. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Checking a sender's identity and request using appropriate technical evidence and trusted channels.
after.mechanism: Inspect authenticated domain signals and confirm sensitive requests independently when risk warrants it.
after.conditions: Useful for targeted messages that exploit familiarity or current business details.
after.limitations: A compromised legitimate mailbox can pass domain checks. Authentic sender identity does not prove benign intent.
after.example: An engineer confirms a sensitive document request with the known project lead through an established channel.

before.expanded_definition: Detects and blocks known or suspected cyber threats.
before.learning_explanation: Threat Protection is a defensive measure described in the source as: Detects and blocks known or suspected cyber threats. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: A broad category of controls that identify or block malicious content and activity.
after.mechanism: Specify the actual product capability, telemetry, prevention policy and response process rather than relying on the label.
after.conditions: Useful when a concrete threat path and supported detection or blocking function are identified.
after.limitations: The term is not a standardized guarantee. Unknown attacks, missing visibility and configuration gaps can defeat coverage.
after.example: A mail-and-endpoint deployment links a malicious attachment alert to containment of the affected workstation.

before.expanded_definition: Practice activities that imitate real security incidents.
before.learning_explanation: Simulated Exercises is a defensive measure described in the source as: Practice activities that imitate real security incidents. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Controlled practice of security decisions and response procedures.
after.mechanism: Use authorized scenarios with defined learning goals, safe execution and constructive feedback.
after.conditions: Useful for rehearsing phishing reporting, verification and incident escalation before a real event.
after.limitations: A simulation does not authenticate a real request or prove future immunity. Exercises must not harm operations or shame individuals.
after.example: A team rehearses independent verification of a tailored supplier-payment request.

before.expanded_definition: Blocks access to harmful or suspicious websites.
before.learning_explanation: Web Filter is a defensive measure described in the source as: Blocks access to harmful or suspicious websites. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Rules controlling access to web destinations or selected web content.
after.mechanism: Block known harmful sites or categories through an assessed proxy, resolver or endpoint enforcement point.
after.conditions: Useful for restricting access to a known compromised site while incident response proceeds.
after.limitations: New destinations, encrypted visibility limits and policy bypasses can reduce coverage. A permitted site can still be malicious.
after.example: A known watering-hole site is temporarily blocked for managed browsers during investigation.

before.expanded_definition: Endpoint Detection and Response — watches devices for suspicious activity.
before.learning_explanation: EDR is a defensive measure described in the source as: Endpoint Detection and Response — watches devices for suspicious activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Collection and analysis of endpoint activity with investigation and response capabilities.
after.mechanism: Correlate process, file, identity and network behavior and support actions such as containment.
after.conditions: Useful for investigating activity that signatures alone may miss when telemetry and staff coverage are sufficient.
after.limitations: Blind spots, tampering and alert overload remain possible. An installed agent is not evidence that every attack is prevented.
after.example: A browser exploit leads to unusual process behavior, prompting endpoint isolation and forensic review.

before.expanded_definition: Checks systems or files for vulnerabilities, threats or suspicious activity.
before.learning_explanation: Scanning is a defensive measure described in the source as: Checks systems or files for vulnerabilities, threats or suspicious activity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Inspection of files, systems or configurations for specified threats or weaknesses.
after.mechanism: Use an appropriate vulnerability, malware or configuration scanner and verify findings in context.
after.conditions: Useful for identifying known problems before deployment or during investigation.
after.limitations: Scanning scope and signatures limit coverage; unknown behavior and unsafe device classes may be missed. A clean result is not proof of safety.
after.example: A removable file is scanned in a controlled environment before an approved transfer.

before.expanded_definition: Allows only approved programs, devices or activities to run or connect.
before.learning_explanation: Allow Listing is a defensive measure described in the source as: Allows only approved programs, devices or activities to run or connect. Its effectiveness depends on implementation and the specific attack path; it should not be presented as a universal prevention guarantee.

after.definition: Execution policy permitting only approved applications or code identities.
after.mechanism: Rules based on assessed publishers, hashes or other supported attributes limit what can run.
after.conditions: Useful on managed systems with controlled software needs and a maintained approval process.
after.limitations: Approved interpreters and signed vulnerable tools can be abused. Overbroad publisher rules or weak administration reduce protection.
after.example: A managed workstation refuses an unapproved fake support utility despite a user's attempt to run it.
